newsitem.title: USA: Babylon, NY says told investors had diverted funds.
newsitem.headline: Babylon, NY says told investors had diverted funds.

text.p: Babylon, N.Y., which has had five of its officials indicted for falsifying vouchers, denied the charges, adding that the town had fully disclosed loans from its capital program faulted by the state monitor.

"I'm absolutely confident that these people will be vindicated because he (the Suffolk County District Attorney) has absolutely no case," said the town supervisor, Richard Schaffer. He added the federal Securities and Exchange Commission had made no effort to contact the town in the matter, nor did he expect it to.

A spokesman for the District Attorney, James Catterson, was not immediately available to comment. The charges, which stemmed from an audit by the state comptroller, say the town officials falsified records to prove part of a $125 million bond sale was used to pay town employees for working on a waste project the offering funded.
Babylon said H. Carl McCall, the comptroller, in a July, 1996 review, sought documentation to show that the town employees and equipment were properly used.

"The comptroller's office said the town did not keep records of all of the equipment and work used, and asked us to provide our best estimate, and we did that," Schaffer said, adding his office has produced 13 cases of such material.

McCall, in the audit last year, also told the town to repay to the waste facilities capital project over $6 million that was loaned to the general fund, highway repair and maintenance fund, and highway machinery fund.

A town official, who requested anonymity, said that the loans from the capital fund from the 1993 sale of $125 million sale of general obligation bonds had been fully disclosed to bond investors. The bond proceeds were earmarked for the town landfill, recycling, and building ash fills.

"In official documents for issuing bonds, in rolling over bonds, we've always told the bonding community. We have a plan of payback clearly laid out," he said, adding the town's strategy was most recently contained in a prospectus for its sale last month of $18.2 million of general obligation bonds.

While such loans are frowned upon by fiscal monitors, the town official said they often were due to delays in getting state aid. The official added that they were common, especially in Long Island's Suffolk County, where Babylon is located, about halfway between New York City and Montauk at the tip of the island. "It is a regular feature of the comptroller's review of Suffolk towns' audited statements."

Babylon next week plans to sell asset-backed beach revenues to a firm that will pay the town about $7.2 million upfront in return for the right to collect the money over the next 25 years. The money will be used to repay the loans from the capital program. "It's specifically to plug that hole," the town official said.
